Training log

2 sessions a week + an optional third · about 45–50 min each

Goal: Lose fat, build strength and definition. Target ~74 kg lean, not 71 kg soft.
Version 2 (Oct 2026). Day A and Day B are the week; Day C is a bonus. Run A → B in order, whatever days you make it. Zero is the only bad number.
⌂

Warm-up

5 minutes. Every session, no exceptions. This is where you protect the shoulder and the hamstring.

⏱
Rowing machine
5–10 min
  • Legs first, then hips, then arms. Reverse that on the way back.
  • Easy pace — you should be able to talk. This is a warm-up, not the workout.
  • 10 min on days you have the full hour, 5 min when you are on 45.

Why: You said you like starting on the rower, and it is a genuinely good choice: full body, warms the hips and upper back, and it is on the machine floor where you start anyway. Keep it easy — the point is blood flow, not a session before the session.

start / end
Cat–Cow
8 slow reps
  • Move one vertebra at a time.
  • Exhale as you round, inhale as you arch.

Why: Wakes up a spine that has been in a desk chair all day.

start / end
Single-leg glute bridge
8 / side
  • Push through the heel.
  • Squeeze the glute at the top, do not arch the lower back.
  • Do the RIGHT side first and pay attention to what the hamstring says.

Why: Gets the glute firing so the hamstring stops doing the glute's job — this is usually the actual fix for a hamstring that stays tight for months.

start / end
Band pull-apart / light face pull
15 reps
  • Light band. Elbows high.
  • Pull to the forehead, thumbs back.

Why: Primes the rear shoulder and rotator cuff before you press anything.

Do not skip this. Five minutes here is the difference between a shoulder that improves over three months and one that does not.

Day A · Push & Squat

Monday. Row 5 min, rehab block, then work down the page. Machine floor only.

Rehab block · first, right after the warm-up
First 6 minutes, straight after the row. This is the part that changes the shoulder and the hamstring, and it only happens if you do it before you are tired and short of time. Light weight, slow, right side first and last.
start / end
Band external rotation
2 × 15 / side
  • Elbow pinned to your side, forearm rotates out.
  • Very light band, slow and controlled. If your arm is swinging, the band is too heavy.
  • Do the right side first and last.

Why: Directly trains the infraspinatus and teres minor — the two small muscles that stop the shoulder pinching when you press. This is the highest-value 90 seconds for your right shoulder.

start / end
Scapular pull-up (hang & shrug down)
2 × 8
  • Hang from the bar, arms straight the whole time.
  • Pull the shoulder blades DOWN without bending the elbows. Tiny movement.
  • If hanging bothers the shoulder, skip it — do band pull-aparts instead.

Why: Teaches the shoulder blade to move properly on the ribcage. Most desk-worker shoulder pain is a scapular control problem wearing a rotator-cuff costume.

start / end
Single-leg glute bridge
2 × 12 / side
  • Slow, 2 seconds up, 2 seconds down.
  • Squeeze at the top. Ribs down.
  • Compare the sides honestly — the right will likely be weaker. That is the finding, not the failure.

Why: Closes the loop on the hamstring: when the glute does its job, the hamstring stops being permanently on duty. This is the difference between managing the problem and fixing it.

Pair 1 · 3 rounds · 90 s rest after the row
start / end
Chest press machine
3 × 6–10
Start at: 50–52 kg — last time 47.3 kg × 10 on every set
Form cues & why it is here
  • Use the vertical / neutral handles if the machine has them. Not the wide horizontal bar.
  • Set the seat so the handles are at mid-chest, not up by your collarbones.
  • Stop when your hands are level with your chest — do not let the elbows travel behind your torso.
  • Push, do not lock out hard at the end.
Why: Same job as the dumbbell press, on the machine floor. A fixed path means you can push closer to your limit without a spotter — but it also means the machine chooses the path, not your shoulder. If the right shoulder complains, the dumbbells are still the safer tool.
If the machine is busy: DB bench press, neutral grip, 2 × 12–14 kg — free-weights floor. Use this whenever the shoulder is grumpy.

Seated cable row
3 × 8–12
Start at: 49.6 kg — get 12 on every set, then go up
Form cues & why it is here
  • Chest up, do not rock backwards to move the weight.
  • Pull the elbows past the ribs, pause one second.
  • Let the shoulder blades travel forward on the way out.
Why: Direct antidote to a research posture. Also builds the mid-back that makes the shoulder feel stable.
If the machine is busy: Chest-supported machine row

Pair 2 · 3 rounds · 90 s rest after the curl
start / end
Hack squat machine
3 × 8–10
Start at: 40 kg — last time 37.5 kg × 10 on every set
Form cues & why it is here
  • Feet mid-platform, shoulder width, toes slightly out.
  • Back flat against the pad the whole time — that is the point of this machine.
  • Go as deep as you can without the lower back peeling off the pad.
  • Push through the whole foot, not the toes.
Why: Same job as the goblet squat with the back supported, and it lives on the machine floor so Day A never leaves it. The pad takes the spinal load out of the movement, which after eight hours at a desk is the version worth doing.
If the machine is busy: Goblet squat, 12–14 kg dumbbell or kettlebell — free-weights floor. Or leg press.

Lying leg curl
3 × 10–12
Start at: 36 kg — 3 seconds on the way down
Form cues & why it is here
  • Slow on the way back down: 3 seconds.
  • Both legs together. Do not let the right leg cheat.
  • Mild pulling in the hamstring is fine. Sharp or pinching is not — stop.
Why: THE most important exercise on this page for you. A hamstring that has been tight for months is usually weak, not short. Loading it is the treatment; stretching it is not.
If the machine is busy: Seated leg curl (often better tolerated)

Pair 3 · 3 rounds · 60 s rest after the rear-delt raise
start / end
Hip thrust
3 × 10–12
Start at: 30–40 kg on the Booty Builder — a weight you could do 14 with
Form cues & why it is here
  • Shoulder blades on the bench, chin tucked.
  • Drive through the heels, squeeze at the top for one second.
  • Ribs down — do not arch the lower back to get higher.
Why: Strong glutes take load off the hamstring. This is the other half of the hamstring fix.
If the machine is busy: Barbell glute bridge on the floor

Reverse pec-deck (rear delt machine)
2 × 15
Start at: 15–20 kg
Form cues & why it is here
  • Chest flat against the pad, arms almost straight.
  • Lead with the elbows and squeeze the shoulder blades together.
  • Stop level with your shoulders — no further back than that.
  • Slow on the way back in. This is not a heavy lift.
Why: Rear delts and upper back, seated and supported, on a stack you can actually add weight to. The external-rotation half of the old exercise now happens in the rehab block, so you get that work three times a week instead of once.
If the machine is busy: Cable rear delt fly — stand between two towers, cables crossed, pull out and back. Or a seated rear-delt row on any machine with a chest pad.

If there is time · 2 rounds · 45 s rest
start / end
Calf press machine
2 × 12–15
Start at: 44 kg — last time 39 kg × 15
Form cues & why it is here
  • Balls of the feet on the bottom edge of the plate, knees soft but fixed.
  • Full range: heels all the way back, then push all the way up.
  • Pause one second at the top.
  • Slow down — calves respond to time under tension, not bouncing.
Why: Calves take load off the hamstring during walking and running, and they are the one muscle that never gets trained by sitting.
If the machine is busy: Calf press on the leg press, or seated calf raise

start / end
Triceps pushdown — rope
2 × 12
Start at: 18 kg — get 12 on both sets, then go up
Form cues & why it is here
  • Elbows pinned to the ribs — they do not travel.
  • Spread the rope apart at the bottom.
  • Rope, not a straight bar: kinder to the elbows and the shoulder.
Why: Triceps are two thirds of the arm. This is the cheapest visible-definition work there is, and it costs the shoulder nothing.
If the machine is busy: Overhead rope extension (only if the shoulder is quiet)

Core · 2 rounds · 45 s rest
start / end
Dead bug
2 × 10 / side
Start at: 16 kg held in both hands — last time 16 kg × 10
Form cues & why it is here
  • Lie on your back, hold a dumbbell or plate over your chest with straight arms.
  • Knees up at 90°. Lower one leg until the heel almost touches the floor, bring it back, switch.
  • Lower back stays pressed into the floor the whole time. If it lifts, shorten the range or go lighter.
  • Slow. Exhale as the leg goes out.
Why: Core that carries over to lifting and to carrying a 3-year-old. The weight overhead makes the abs work harder to keep the ribs down.
If the floor is busy: Pallof press on a cable, 2 × 10 / side.

Free-weight floor · 3 sets · 2 min rest

Romanian deadlift
3 × 8
Start at: 37.5 kg, then 40 when all 8s are clean — last time 35 kg × 8
Form cues & why it is here
  • Push the hips BACK, do not bend forward.
  • Soft knees, bar stays touching the legs.
  • Stop when the hamstrings say stop — usually mid-shin, not the floor.
  • Right side is the one to watch. Any sharp pull, drop the weight.
Why: The single best long-term fix for that hamstring — but only if you earn the load. Add weight slower than you want to.
If the machine is busy: Dumbbell RDL, or single-leg RDL with light dumbbell

Lat pulldown
3 × 8–10
Start at: 51.5–52 kg — last time 49.6 kg × 10 on every set
Form cues & why it is here
  • Use a shoulder-width or neutral grip, not the widest one — kinder to the right shoulder.
  • Pull to the collarbone, never behind the neck.
  • Lead with the elbows.
Why: Builds the V-shape that reads as 'definition' faster than almost anything else.

Incline chest press machine
3 × 8–10
Start at: 34–36 kg — last time 32 kg × 10 on every set
Form cues & why it is here
  • Neutral / vertical handles if available.
  • Seat high enough that the handles sit at upper chest.
  • Stop level with the chest. Never let the elbows drift behind you.
  • Slow on the way in, controlled on the way out.
Why: Upper chest and front delts without needing an adjustable bench. The incline angle is fixed and shallow, which is exactly what a cranky right shoulder wants.
If the machine is busy: Incline DB press, neutral grip, 30°, 2 × 10–12 kg — free-weights floor.

Split squat
3 × 8 / side
Start at: 2 × 8–10 kg dumbbells
Form cues & why it is here
  • Long stance, back knee drops straight down.
  • Front shin fairly vertical, weight through the front heel.
  • Hold a rack or wall for balance at first — no shame.
Why: Single-leg work exposes and fixes the left/right imbalance that is very likely feeding the right hamstring problem.
If the machine is busy: Reverse lunge, or step-up onto a low box

Seated leg curl
3 × 12–15
Start at: 41–44 kg — last time 39 kg × 15 on every set
Form cues & why it is here
  • 3 seconds on the way back out. The slow part is the point.
  • Hips stay down in the seat.
  • This is the second hamstring exercise of the day on purpose. Keep it light.
Why: Seated leg curl trains the hamstring at a longer muscle length than the lying version — the position where it is most likely to complain. Best single exercise for a stubborn hamstring.
If the machine is busy: Lying leg curl at a lighter weight

Cable lateral raise
2 × 12–15
Start at: 3.4 kg — 4.5 kg was too big a jump (you got 8). Earn it back with 15s
Form cues & why it is here
  • One arm at a time, low pulley, cable crossing in front of you.
  • Lead with the elbow, stop at shoulder height.
  • Light. If you are shrugging, it is too heavy.
Why: Side delts, on the functional trainer, so the whole back half of Day B stays on one floor. The cable keeps tension at the bottom where dumbbells give you nothing.
If the machine is busy: Dumbbell lateral raise, 2 × 5–6 kg — free-weights floor.

2 × 15
Start at: 13.5 kg — get all 15 reps before going heavier
Form cues & why it is here
  • Rope at forehead height.
  • Pull apart AND back, thumbs finishing behind the ears.

Curls are paused for four weeks because the right inner elbow still complains. Rows and pulldowns already train the biceps. If the elbow is still sore by then, mention it at the same physio visit as the hamstring.
Core · 3 rounds · 45 s rest
start / end
Hanging knee raise
3 × 8–12
Start at: Bodyweight
Form cues & why it is here
  • Hang from the Chin Assist frame, shoulders down and away from your ears.
  • Curl the knees up and the pelvis under — it is a curl, not a leg lift.
  • No swinging. If you swing, do fewer reps.
Why: The strongest ab exercise available to you, and it decompresses the spine at the same time — a good thing after a day at a desk.
If the machine is busy: Lying leg raise on a mat, or the Abdominal Machine.

Conditioning · first, while you are fresh
start / end
Intervals — rower or bike
8 × (30 s hard / 60 s easy)
  • 2 min easy first, then 8 rounds, then 1 min easy. 14 minutes in total.
  • Hard means breathing hard but still in control — about 8 out of 10, not a sprint to collapse.
  • Bike if the right hamstring is grumbling that day; rower otherwise.

Why: This is what the classes were giving you — heart and lungs, and calories — in a third of the time, without tiring the muscles you need for Monday.

Glutes · 3 rounds · 60 s rest
start / end
Hip abduction machine
3 × 15
Start at: 30–40 kg
Form cues & why it is here
  • Sit tall, lean very slightly forward.
  • Push the knees apart slowly and hold a beat at the widest point.
  • Control the way back in — do not let the stack drop.
Why: This trains the glute medius, the side glute almost nobody trains. A weak glute medius is one of the standard reasons a hamstring ends up overworked and permanently tight on one side.
If the machine is busy: Band walks: loop a band above the knees and side-step 15 m each way.

Cable glute kickback
2 × 12 / side
Start at: 10–15 kg
Form cues & why it is here
  • Ankle strap on the low pulley, hands on the frame.
  • Drive the leg straight back from the hip, squeeze at the top.

Why: Isolated glute max, one side at a time, so the weaker side cannot hide behind the stronger one. Start with your right.
If the machine is busy: Bodyweight glute kickback on all fours, or a single-leg hip thrust.

Hotel · Full body dumbbells

For travel weeks. Same workout both times, at least one day apart. About 40 minutes. Weights are per hand. Saved like any other day, but it does not move the A/B/C rotation.

This is your deload. The log says week 8 is the deload week, and the conference lands right on it — perfect timing. Leave 3 reps in the tank on every set. You are keeping the habit and the movement patterns, not chasing numbers. Second session: add 1–2 reps per set, not weight.
Warm-up · 5 min, no band needed
3 min on any cardio machine (or brisk marching in place) → World's greatest stretch 3 / side → 10 slow arm circles each way → 10 bodyweight squats. If you pack a mini band (it weighs nothing), do the normal Warm-up tab instead.
start / end
Side-lying DB external rotation
2 × 15 / side
  • Lie on your left side on a bench or the floor, a folded towel between your right elbow and ribs.
  • Elbow bent 90°, rotate the forearm up towards the ceiling, slowly down.
  • Tiny weight: 1–2 kg, or a full water bottle. Right side first and last.

Why: The hotel version of the band external rotation. Same muscles (infraspinatus, teres minor), no band needed — keeps the shoulder routine going while you are away.

start / end
Single-leg glute bridge
2 × 12 / side
  • Slow, 2 seconds up, 2 seconds down.
  • Squeeze at the top. Ribs down.
  • Right side first.

Why: Wakes the glutes up before the hinge, so the right hamstring is not left doing their job.

Pair 1 · 3 rounds · go straight from one to the other, 75 s rest after the row
start / end
DB goblet squat
3 × 10–12
Start at: 16–20 kg (one dumbbell, held at the chest)
Form cues & why it is here
  • Hold one dumbbell vertically against your chest, elbows pointing down.
  • Sit down between your heels, chest tall, knees track over the toes.
  • Go as deep as you can with a neutral back, drive up through the whole foot.
Why: Replaces the hack squat. Holding the weight in front keeps you upright, which is easy on the lower back and still hits the quads hard. Your hack squat went from 30 to 37.5 kg in a month — 12 kg goblet from August is long outgrown.
If the dumbbells are too light: Go slower instead of heavier — 3 seconds down, a 1-second pause, and add reps up to 15. Slow reps with a light weight are a real training stimulus.

DB one-arm row
3 × 10–12 / side
Start at: 18–20 kg
Form cues & why it is here
  • One hand and knee on a bench — or, with no bench, stagger your stance and rest a hand on a rack or chair.
  • Pull the dumbbell towards your hip, not your armpit. Shoulder blade back and down.
  • Right side first. Pause 1 second at the top.
Why: Replaces the seated cable row and lat pulldown. Your cable row is around 50 kg now, so the 12.5 kg you used in August is far too light — start at 18–20.
If the dumbbells are too light: Go slower instead of heavier — 3 seconds down, a 1-second pause, and add reps up to 15. Slow reps with a light weight are a real training stimulus.

Pair 2 · 3 rounds · 75 s rest after the press
start / end
DB Romanian deadlift
3 × 10
Start at: 2 × 14–16 kg
Form cues & why it is here
  • Dumbbells in front of the thighs, soft knees.
  • Push the hips back, slide the weights down the legs. 3 seconds down.
  • Stop when you feel the hamstrings stretch — not when the back rounds. Usually just below the knee.
  • If the right hamstring gives a sharp tug, shorten the range. A stretch is fine, a pull is not.
Why: Keeps the hinge pattern and the hamstring loading going. Your barbell RDL is 35 kg; 2 × 14–16 kg is a deliberate step down for a deload week.
If the dumbbells are too light: Go slower instead of heavier — 3 seconds down, a 1-second pause, and add reps up to 15. Slow reps with a light weight are a real training stimulus.

start / end
DB floor press — neutral grip
3 × 10–12
Start at: 2 × 16–18 kg
Form cues & why it is here
  • Lie on the floor, knees bent, palms facing each other.
  • Lower until the upper arms touch the floor, pause, press up.
  • Elbows at about 45° from the body, not flared out.
Why: The floor stops the elbows at a depth that keeps the right shoulder out of trouble. That makes this the most shoulder-friendly press you can do with dumbbells. A bench is fine too, but the floor is kinder.
If the dumbbells are too light: Go slower instead of heavier — 3 seconds down, a 1-second pause, and add reps up to 15. Slow reps with a light weight are a real training stimulus.

DB reverse lunge
2 × 8–10 / side
Start at: 2 × 8–10 kg
Form cues & why it is here
  • Step back, lower until the back knee almost touches the floor.
  • Front shin stays fairly vertical, push back up through the front heel.
  • Do all reps on one side, then switch. Right leg in front first.
Why: Single-leg work — the part of the programme you miss most often, because Day C rarely happens. Stepping back is easier on the knees than a forward lunge.
If balance is a problem: Hold one dumbbell only and keep a hand on the rack.

Class

Stram op or anything else you drop into. Log it so your week counts honestly.

You are running this right. 3–5 kg, not pushing — that keeps Stram op as conditioning and movement practice rather than a third and fourth strength session. At that load it will not eat Tuesday or Thursday, which is the whole point. The lifting is what drives your progress; the class is for enjoyment, conditioning and getting more practice under a barbell with someone watching your technique.
Watch for the weight creeping up. At 3–5 kg the deadlift and squat blocks are a movement drill and your hamstring is in no danger. The risk is drift: a month in, the room is using 10 kg and so are you, without ever deciding to. Going heavier is a decision to make deliberately — and not before the anaemia has resolved. Log the effort each time; if “Hard” starts appearing, that is the signal.

Desk breaks & hamstring homework

Non-negotiable on non-gym days. Two minutes, twice a day. This matters more than any single gym session for how your body feels.

start / end
Glute bridge
2 × 12

Why: Every morning, before the day starts. Wakes the glutes up so they — not the hamstring — do the work when you stand, walk and lift. This is the highest-value two minutes in the whole plan.

start / end
World’s greatest stretch
5 / side

Why: Hip flexors, hamstring, thoracic spine and shoulder in one movement. If you only do one thing on a non-gym day, do this.

start / end
Chest & front-of-shoulder stretch
40 s / side

Why: Eight hours of typing shortens the front of the shoulder and quietly pulls it into the position that hurts. Undo it in a doorway, twice a day.

start / end
Cat–Cow
10 reps

Why: Resets a spine that has held one shape too long. Do it on the floor while the little one plays.

start / end
Calf stretch at the wall
45 s / side

Why: Tight calves change how the hamstring loads with every step you take. Cheap fix, often overlooked.

Nordic / glute-ham raise — NOT YET
Week 9+

Why: The strongest hamstring-injury protector that exists. Do NOT start this now — it would flare the right side. Earn it with eight weeks of leg curls and Romanian deadlifts first, then we add it.

How to run it

The rules that make the difference.

Session shape — 45–50 minutes

Row 5 min → rehab block, 6 min → pair 1 → pair 2 → pair 3 → core. Do the two exercises of a pair back to back, then rest. Warm-up and rehab stay under 12 minutes; the lifting is the rest.

The rehab block moved to the front on purpose. It used to sit at the end, which is exactly where things get cut when you are short of time — and it is the one part that is actually treating the shoulder and the hamstring. At the front it costs you six minutes of a session you have already committed to.

The week. Mon Day A · Wed Day B · Fri Day C (optional) · weekends off. Every muscle gets trained twice a week on A and B alone, which is enough to keep getting stronger. Day C adds the conditioning the classes used to give you.

When time runs out, cut the "if there is time" pair first, then core. Never the rehab block.

The week

Alternate A → B → A → B, with at least one day between sessions. Day C only happens once A and B are done that week — it never replaces one of them. If you miss Monday, do A on Wednesday; the queue just moves along. Nothing is ever "lost".

A realistic week with a 3-year-old: two sessions is a win, three is a great week. The plan survives either.

How to add weight — double progression

Do not add weight every session. Do this instead:

  • Stay at the same weight until you hit the top of the rep range on every set.
  • Then add 2.5 kg (upper body) or 5 kg (legs) and drop back to the bottom of the range.
  • Repeat. That is the whole system.

Leave 1–2 reps in the tank on every set. You should finish a session thinking "I could have done a bit more". Training to failure at 42 with a bad shoulder buys fatigue, not muscle.

WeeksFocusWhat changes
1–2Learn the patternsDeliberately light. Get the movements clean. Expect soreness.
3–6BuildWeight climbs steadily. This is where strength shows up.
7–8ConsolidateOne easier week. Same exercises, ~70% of the weight, same reps.
v2From 12 OctTwo main days, heavier main lifts (6–10 reps), optional flex day. Deload again after six weeks.

Cardio — do less than you think

The fat loss comes from the kitchen and from daily movement, not from the treadmill. The highest-leverage change for a researcher is steps: aim for 8,000–10,000 a day. Walk the little one instead of driving. Take calls standing.

If you want structured cardio, add one 25–30 min easy session (bike, brisk walk, swim) on a non-gym day. Keep it easy enough to hold a conversation. Anything harder eats into your recovery for the lifting, which is what is actually reshaping you.

The right hamstring — read this once. A hamstring that has felt "contracted" for months is almost never short. It is usually under-strong and over-worked because the glute on that side is not pulling its weight. Stretching it aggressively tends to make it worse. What fixes it: leg curls, Romanian deadlifts and hip thrusts, loaded progressively over 8–12 weeks, plus glute bridges every morning. Give it eight honest weeks. If it is still there, or if you ever get sharp pain or pain that refers down the back of the leg, see a physiotherapist — that is worth far more than any gym add-on.
The right shoulder. Every pressing movement here is deliberately neutral-grip and stops short of the deep range. Rear-delt work (reverse pec-deck on A, face pulls on B) is in both main days on purpose. Rule of thumb: a dull ache during a set that fades by the next day is fine. Pain that is sharp, or that is worse the following morning, means drop the weight or swap the exercise. Nothing in this plan is worth an injured shoulder.

Tracking your body

Weigh-ins, tape measurements and the weekly check-in live in the separate Daily log page, alongside the food log. Weigh three mornings a week; measure the waist once a week. Read the trend line, never a single day.

Because you are lifting, the waist will often move before the scale does. That is the plan working, not failing.

Logging

Fill in kg and reps as you go, tick each set off (it starts the rest timer automatically), then tap Copy log at the end and paste it into the Fitness chat with Claude. That builds your history and lets the plan adapt to what you are actually lifting.
